extracted.intended_audience: poets, essayists, and writers interested in description, landscape/architectural aesthetics, and imaginative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing descriptive and imaginative writing (poetry/prose) and for designing scenes (gardens, architecture) that most strongly affect the reader's imagination. Covers principles of grandeur, novelty, form, use of words, and techniques for fantastic/fairy writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden design: naturalism over formal geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for plantations and grounds that 'strike the Imagination at first Sight' by humouring Nature rather than laying out Trees in equal Rows and uniform Figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessively regular, mathematically trimmed shapes ('Trees rise in Cones, Globes, and Pyramids' / 'Marks of the Scissars upon every Plant'). Prefer luxuriancy and diffusion of boughs; improve natural embroidery of meadows with small additions of art; set off hedges and fields with trees and flowers that the soil can support. Beware the gardener's commercial tendency to tear up productive plantings for fashionable parterres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness in architecture: bulk (scale) and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness may relate either to the bulk/body of the structure or to the manner in which it is built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulk (immense scale) impresses by magnitude (examples: Tower of Babel, Walls of Babylon, Egyptian pyramids, Wall of China). Manner (distribution, proportion, and style) can make a small building produce nobler ideas than a much larger but meanly-mannered one — thus aim for greatness of manner even when scale is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of manner: few large principal members, avoid small distracting ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: To introduce Grandeur of Manner, 'the Division of the Principal Members of the Order may consist but of few Parts, that they be all great and of a bold and ample Relievo... that the Eye, beholding nothing little and mean, the Imagination may be more vigorously touched.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make principal elements bold and ample; avoid redundancy of smaller ornaments (quarter rounds, numerous cavings) that scatter the eye and reduce solemn effect. Example: in a cornice prefer graceful projections and noble show over an intermixture of many little particulars that create confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concave/convex and round forms to impart magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all the Figures in Architecture, 'none... have a greater Air than the Concave and the Convex' and round pillars and vaulted roofs form a great part of buildings designed for pomp and magnificence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domes, arches, round pillars and vaults because they present more of a continuous surface to the eye (the eye can take in the whole concavity at once), producing a unified, majestic impression. Arches open the sky and give grander prospects than square openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape and sight: make forms that the eye can take in at once
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is more struck where the eye can grasp a uniform idea (e.g., inside of a dome) than where sight must split on several angles (square pillar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design elements so they form unified visual ideas rather than many small, competing planes; prefer figures whose surfaces the eye can surround or collect into one impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words can evoke more vivid ideas than immediate sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, when well chosen, have so great a Force in them, that a Description often gives us more lively Ideas than the Sight of Things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer can 'give as free a View as he pleases' by selecting and amplifying parts of a scene; use precise, energetic, and well-weighted word choices to raise complex or heightened images that may outstrip direct perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary pleasures of the imagination arise from comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure comes from the mind's action which compares ideas raised by words (representations) with ideas from the original objects; this comparison produces delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the reader's faculty to compare representation and original — well-timed, apt descriptions that echo or improve what the reader knows will give satisfaction. Even disagreeable objects (a dunghill) can please when aptly represented, because of the aptness of the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of novelty and strangeness to affect the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing in this whole Art which pleases the Imagination, but as it is Great, Uncommon, or Beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new, surprising, or strange elements (Ovid's miracles, Milton's strange creations) to arrest the imagination. But novelty must be balanced — the poet may 'mend and perfect Nature' to delight but should avoid absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stir passions (terror and pity) carefully to increase pleasure by reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The two leading Passions which the more serious Parts of Poetry endeavour to stir up in us, are Terror and Pity; these are pleasurable in description because we reflect we are not in danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing fearful or distressing scenes, allow the reader psychological distance so reflection (sense of safety or comparison with self) can convert horror into an agreeable emotional exercise. Do not press the object so close as to remove possibility of reflective pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: A strong imagination and precise knowledge of language are required
rubrics_metrics.description: Different readers have different relish of the same descriptions because of the 'Perfection of Imagination' and the 'different Ideas that several Readers affix to the same Words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should cultivate their own imagination and mastery of expression. Be aware that audience members vary — some will need more vivid, familiar, or explicit cues; skilled diction and well-stocked imaginative inventory helps reach more readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should study diverse models and sources to enrich imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble Writer should 'gain a due Relish of the Works of Nature' and be 'thoroughly conversant' in country scenery, courts' pomp, painting, statuary, architecture and ancient models (Homer, Virgil, Ovid, Milton) to expand his imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely: Homer (greatness/sublime), Virgil (beauty/agreeable), Ovid (strangeness/novel) — use each model's strengths. Practical exposure to varied scenes (country life, courts, ruins) will supply images and figures for richer description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical freedom: combine seasons and elements but avoid absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet has 'the modelling of Nature in his own Hands' and may combine the beauties of different seasons or climates (flowers of spring and autumn together) provided he 'does not reform her too much, and run into Absurdities, by endeavouring to excel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to intensify or compress natural features for heightened effect (simultaneous blossoms, exotic plants) but maintain plausibility and internal coherence to avoid breaking the reader's suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy/fantastical writing requires a peculiar imaginative cast and altered speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Fairy Way of Writing' depends on an imagination 'naturally fruitful and superstitious' and knowledge of legends; spirits should not 'talk like People of his own Species' — their sense ought to be a little discoloured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For credible fantastical characters, cultivate a particular tone and diction (slightly discoloured sense) and draw on legends, fables, and antiquated romances. Avoid making supernatural beings converse as ordinary humans; give them a distinct mental cast and idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and management of revelation in description (Ovid's technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ovid's art consists 'chiefly in well-timing his Description, before the first Shape is quite worn off, and the new one perfectly finished' so that he entertains readers with something unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control the pace at which images are revealed: introduce partial transformations or hints to sustain wonder, revealing details at moments that maximize surprise and imaginative effect rather than all at once.
